guest.bio_context: Peter White is an Indigenous iron worker and journeyman tradesperson from the Tanaka people with family connections to the Tulalip, Sniquami, Skykomish, and Duwamish tribes. He has over 12 years of sobriety (as of June 15th) and worked extensively in the oil and gas sector in Fort McMurray, Alberta, before transitioning to structural iron work. He survived cancer of the foot and underwent multiple surgeries while maintaining his career in the trades, and has since reconnected deeply with his Indigenous cultural practices including powwow dancing.

pending_qa.q: What occupational adjustments did an iron worker make after major foot surgery and recovery?
pending_qa.r: After surgery where tendons from his two middle toes were severed and attached to his big toe, and multiple veins were closed off, Peter had to learn to walk again. When he became a journeyman, he was able to secure work with IATSE at Rheingroup, which kept him busy and allowed him to get back on his feet in an easier way than returning to rebar or general construction. He notes that both his red seals (certifications) require physically demanding work, and he has witnessed others forced to completely change careers after similar injuries.

pending_qa.q: Why is community support essential to preventing relapse in early sobriety, according to a recovered tradesperson?
pending_qa.r: Peter emphasizes that if you don't have an uplifting, supporting community, you will end up relapsing and failing. Community was the big thing for him during recovery—meeting new people, learning new things, and figuring out who he was as an Indigenous person. His time dealing with cancer and foot surgery unexpectedly reconnected him with community when he felt most lost, which he now recognizes as essential to his sustained sobriety.
